cheatSheet.oneLineDefinition: Capacity planning quantifies resource demand from throughput targets and growth forecasts; autoscaling matches supply to demand dynamically so data pipelines maintain SLAs without over-provisioning.
keyConcepts: Little's Law: L = λ * W (concurrency = arrival_rate * sojourn_time).
USE method: Utilization, Saturation, Errors for every resource.
Utilization formula: ρ = λ * service_time; keep ρ < 0.70 for headroom.
Spark dynamic allocation requires external shuffle service.
Kafka partition count is immutable—provision for 2-4x peak at creation.
Four Spark bottleneck types: CPU, memory/GC, I/O/spill, shuffle/skew.
formulas: Utilization: ρ = arrival_rate * service_time = λ / μ
M/M/1 queue length: L = ρ / (1 - ρ)  [blows up as ρ → 1]
Required Kafka partitions: ceil(target_mb_per_s / per_partition_mb_per_s * safety_factor)
commands: Kafka producer benchmark: kafka-producer-perf-test.sh --topic T --num-records 5000000 --record-size 1024 --throughput -1 --producer-props bootstrap.servers=... acks=1
Flink cancel with savepoint: flink cancel -s s3://bucket/savepoints/ <jobId>
Snowflake suspend warehouse: ALTER WAREHOUSE my_wh SUSPEND;
Snowflake query history: SELECT * FROM SNOWFLAKE.ACCOUNT_USAGE.QUERY_HISTORY WHERE TOTAL_ELAPSED_TIME > 30000 ORDER BY START_TIME DESC LIMIT 100;
Prometheus recording rule reload: curl -X POST http://prometheus:9090/-/reload
KEDA check ScaledObject: kubectl describe scaledobject flink-taskmanager-scaler -n data-platform
interviewPoints: Apply USE (Utilization/Saturation/Errors) to every resource before concluding you need more capacity.
Little's Law converts throughput + latency SLOs into parallelism requirements.
Kafka partition counts are immutable—always provision 2-4x peak at creation.
Spark dynamic allocation requires the external shuffle service or shuffleTracking.
KEDA lagThreshold too small causes rebalance storms—derive it from Little's Law.
Keep P95 utilization below 70% (30% headroom) per queuing theory.
Multi-cluster Snowflake scales concurrency; larger warehouse size scales per-query performance—they solve different problems.
quickNotes: Saturation (queue depth) is a leading indicator of failure; utilization alone can look fine while the queue grows.
ρ > 0.8 causes superlinear latency growth in M/M/1 queues—not linear degradation.
Benchmarking per-partition Kafka throughput is essential—do not assume 100 MB/s; measure it on your instance type.
Flink backpressure at operator level means overall parallelism increase does not help—fix the bottleneck operator.
KEDA ScaledJob (not ScaledObject) for batch consumers that should scale to zero between runs.
Snowflake SCALING_POLICY=ECONOMY waits longer before adding clusters; use STANDARD for latency-sensitive workloads.
Warm pools cut EC2 scale-up from 3-8 minutes to 30-60 seconds for batch window SLAs.

keyTakeaways: Little's Law (L = λ * W) and the utilization formula (ρ = λ * service_time) are the mathematical foundations for sizing every data platform component—Spark executor pools, Kafka partitions, Flink task slots, and warehouse concurrency—from first principles rather than guesswork.

The USE method (Utilization, Saturation, Errors) applied systematically to every resource—CPU, memory, disk I/O, network, Kafka lag, Spark shuffle spill, Flink backpressure—prevents missing the actual bottleneck and ensures capacity investments target the binding constraint.

Kafka partition count is effectively immutable in production and is the primary throughput scaling knob; always apply the capacity formula and provision for 2-4x projected peak at topic creation time to avoid a disruptive migration.

Autoscaling policies (KEDA for Kafka-driven workers, Spark dynamic allocation for batch, Snowflake multi-cluster for concurrency) must have their bounds derived from capacity formulas, not set arbitrarily—incorrectly tuned bounds cause thundering-herd rebalances, runaway costs, or SLA misses at exactly the moments when the system is under stress.

Keep P95 resource utilization below 70% as a headroom target: queuing theory shows that latency grows superlinearly (L = ρ / (1-ρ)) as utilization approaches 1, so the last 30% of capacity is not spare room but a necessary buffer against burst traffic.

Capacity planning is a continuous discipline: quarterly forecasting reviews with 6-month growth projections give 30-60 days of warning before resource ceilings are hit, enabling proactive architectural changes (repartitioning, state backend migration) that cannot be done under incident pressure.

The four Spark performance bottleneck types—CPU (algorithmic/serialization), memory (GC/spill), I/O (small files/S3 throttling), and shuffle (skew/excessive partitions)—each require different fixes; adding more executors only helps the CPU-bound case, and blindly scaling compute wastes money without addressing root causes.
